column2: How often customers offer to sell

After you appraise everything a customer brought in, whether they offer to sell it to you depends on the average grade of your appraisals. Chance by average grade (Perfect / Excellent / Good / Mediocre / Awful): Low = 50 / 40 / 30 / 20 / 10 %, Normal = 90 / 75 / 60 / 40 / 20 %, High = 100 / 95 / 85 / 65 / 40 %. Averages in between are interpolated. Nothing is asked when no offer comes.

column2: Haldane was a small watchmaker in the Lower Levels that assembled mechanical wristwatches entirely by hand. It closed after its third and last production run, and no one on the Station has the tools or the patience to build one today.\n\nThis guide will provide everything you need to know to appraise the value of any Haldane watch.
Regardless of condition, a Haldane watch has a base value of 360 Credits, and a minimum value of 120 Credits.
The dial color tells which production run a watch came from. The case metal is read from the bezel and the lugs.
Sub-dials are tiny dials set into the main dial. The harder a movement was to build, the more of them it has.
Watches lose their original hands more often than you might think. Original hands are thick and cream-colored; replacements are thin sticks in a bright yellow.
Every genuine Haldane watch has this emblem printed on its dial, below the 12 o'clock mark: a round ring around an eight-toothed gear with a hole in its center.

If any part of the emblem is different, the watch is counterfeit. A counterfeit never earns the Production Run, Case Metal or Sub-Dial bonus, and is worth -115 Credits.\n\nA dial with the emblem scraped off is not counterfeit, but it was probably stolen. (-65 Credits)
Original Condition If ALL conditions match: - Genuine emblem - Original hands - Crown present - Clean glass +160 Credits

Alder was a small electronics workshop in the Lower Levels that built audio amplifier tubes entirely by hand. It lost its tooling after a third and last production run, and no one on the Station can make a tube like these today.\n\nThis guide will provide everything you need to know to appraise the value of any Alder vacuum tube.
Regardless of condition, an Alder tube has a base value of 250 Credits, and a minimum value of 70 Credits.
The color of the bakelite base tells which production run a tube came from. The older the run, the better it was built.
The getter is the silver mirror inside the glass dome. It soaks up stray gas, and it shows how the tube has lived. A white getter means air has leaked in: the tube is dead.
Haze builds up where the glass has been handled and heated. A crack lets the air in, and a cracked tube is dead.
A tube needs all seven pins to sit in its socket. A bent pin can still work; a pin broken off short cannot.
Every genuine Alder tube has this emblem printed on its glass, below the electrodes: a ring around a single lightning bolt.
If any part of the emblem is different, the tube is counterfeit. A counterfeit never earns the Production Run or Original Condition bonus, and is worth -80 Credits.

Sunvale was an orchard company in the Lower Levels that grew and canned fruit back when the supply lines still ran. Its tins are still turning up in the lower decks, and no one on the Station can make a tin like these today.\n\nThis guide will provide everything you need to know to appraise the value of any Sunvale canned fruit.
Regardless of condition, a Sunvale tin has a base value of 170 Credits, and a minimum value of 30 Credits.
The picture on the label tells which fruit is inside. The rarer the fruit, the more a tin is worth.
How the lid opens tells the generation of the tin. The oldest tins have no opening feature at all and need a can opener. Nobody makes those any more.
Dents show how roughly a tin has been handled. A large dent bends the whole side of the tin.
Rust creeps in at the lid and the rim first, then runs down the sides.
A tin that has swollen has food that has gone bad inside. The lid bulges up into a dome and the sides bulge out. Never eat one.
Every genuine Sunvale tin has this seal stuck on its label, to the lower right of the fruit: a round seal with a sun above a single leaf.
If any part of the seal is different, the tin is counterfeit. A counterfeit never earns the Fruit or Lid bonus, and is worth -35 Credits.

Marlowe was a dairy in the livestock quarter of the Lower Levels that aged hard cheese in wax for years. It closed after only a few batches, and no one on the Station has the pastures or the patience to make a wheel like these today.\n\nThis guide will provide everything you need to know to appraise the value of any Marlowe cheese wheel.
Regardless of condition, a Marlowe wheel has a base value of 500 Credits, and a minimum value of 100 Credits.
The color of the rind tells how long a wheel has aged. The darker the rind, the older and the more valuable the wheel.
Pale Yellow Rind: Aged 3 Years\n(No Change)
Dark Gray Rind: Aged 15 Years\n(+260 Credits)
The seal around the side of the wheel shows which line it came from. Plain red wax is standard; the other two were made in smaller batches.
A soft white bloom on the rind is a good sign. Blue-green spots mean the wheel has turned. Do not eat it.
A hairline crack is only skin deep. A deep crack runs into the paste and lets the air in.
A wheel is worth the most whole. A missing wedge shows the paste inside, with its round holes (eyes).
Every genuine Marlowe wheel has this stamp pressed into its rind, at the back of the top face: a round ring around two wheat ears spreading in a V.
If any part of the stamp is different, the wheel is counterfeit. A counterfeit never earns the Rind or Seal bonus, and is worth -100 Credits.

Fenwick was a model works in the Lower Levels that built working vertical steam engines for hobbyists, to be fired up and run on a workbench, back when the supply lines still ran. It closed after three production runs, and no one on the Station has the patience to build one today.\n\nThis guide will provide everything you need to know to appraise the value of any Fenwick steam engine model.
Regardless of condition, a Fenwick model has a base value of 310 Credits, and a minimum value of 80 Credits.
The finish of the plinth tells which production run a model came from. The metal of the boiler is read from its color.
Dark Wood Plinth: 1st Production Run (Years 380-391)\n(+120 Credits)
Green Enamel Plinth: 2nd Production Run (Years 392-401)\n(+60 Credits)
Gray Steel Plinth: 3rd Production Run (Years 402-410)\n(No Change)
Six thin spokes take the most work to build; a solid cast disc takes the least. A chimney with a flared cap is original; a plain pipe is a replacement.
A model with a holed boiler, a missing gauge or a broken chimney cannot be run.
Every genuine Fenwick model has this brass nameplate on the front of its boiler: a round ring around a piston with a small flywheel under it.
If any part of the nameplate is different, the model is counterfeit. A counterfeit never earns the Production Run or Flywheel bonus, and is worth -90 Credits.
